title: CISA Official Review Manual – 28th Edition
description: A structured summary of all 5 CISA domains with concepts, topics, subtopics, real-life scenarios, examples, and key terminologies for exam preparation.

domains.summary: This domain covers how IS audits are planned, executed, and reported. It forms the backbone of the CISA role — understanding audit standards, risk-based planning, types of controls, evidence collection, and communication of audit results.
domains.real_life_analogy: Think of an IS audit like a health checkup for a company's IT systems. Just as a doctor follows a structured process — reviewing patient history, running tests, and issuing a report — an IS auditor plans, examines controls, gathers evidence, and delivers findings.

topics.topic_name: IS Audit Standards, Guidelines, Functions and Codes of Ethics

subtopics.name: ISACA IS Audit and Assurance Standards
subtopics.summary: Mandatory requirements for IS auditing and reporting. Divided into General, Performance, and Reporting standards.

categories.General: Guiding principles — ethics, independence, objectivity, due care, knowledge and competency.
categories.Performance: Conduct of assignments — planning, supervision, risk, evidence gathering.
categories.Reporting: Types of reports, communication methods, and information to be communicated.

subtopics.key_point: Standards are MANDATORY. Guidelines provide guidance on HOW to apply standards. Tools & Techniques are examples — not requirements.
subtopics.exam_tip: ISACA tests your ability to APPLY standards, not memorize numbering.

subtopics.name: ISACA IS Audit and Assurance Guidelines
subtopics.summary: Provide guidance on how to comply with standards. IS auditors should consider them, use professional judgment, and justify any departure.
subtopics.key_point: Guidelines = guidance. Departure is allowed if professionally justified.

subtopics.name: ISACA Code of Professional Ethics
subtopics.summary: Governs professional and personal conduct of ISACA members and certification holders.
seven_principles: Perform duties with objectivity, due diligence and professional care.
Serve stakeholders lawfully with high standards of conduct.
Maintain privacy and confidentiality of obtained information.
Maintain competency and undertake only tasks within your skill set.
Inform appropriate parties of all significant findings.
subtopics.exam_tip: You don't memorize the ethics code. You understand and APPLY it in scenarios.
subtopics.real_life_scenario: An auditor discovers payroll fraud during an unrelated audit engagement. Ethics require disclosure to appropriate parties even if outside original audit scope.

subtopics.name: IT Assurance Framework (ITAF)
subtopics.summary: A comprehensive best-practice reference model that establishes standards for IS auditor roles, knowledge, skills, and conduct.
subtopics.key_point: ITAF is the framework that organizes standards, guidelines, and tools for IS audit.

subtopics.name: IS Internal Audit Function

key_concepts.Audit Charter: A board-approved document that defines the authority, responsibility, and scope of the IS audit function. It is the auditor's permission slip.
key_concepts.Independence: Internal audit must report to the audit committee or highest management level to remain independent.
key_concepts.Resource Management: IS auditors must continuously update skills due to changing technology. Staff training plans should align with organizational IT direction.
key_concepts.Outsourcing Audits: When using external experts, the IS auditor retains professional liability. External experts must be supervised and their work reviewed.

subtopics.real_life_scenario: Imagine a bank's internal audit team that reports directly to the CFO. This creates independence issues because the CFO controls the budget. Best practice: report to the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors.
subtopics.exam_tip: The Audit Charter grants authority. A request from management does NOT.

topics.topic_name: Types of Audits, Assessments and Reviews

subtopics.name: Types of Audits

types.description: Collects evidence to determine if IS systems are protected, reliable and providing value.
Tests adherence to specific regulations or standards (e.g., PCI-DSS, GDPR).
Assesses accuracy of financial reporting. Focuses on financial data integrity.
Evaluates internal control structure in a given process or area.
Combines financial and operational audit steps. Assesses overall organizational objectives.
Specialized audit to discover fraudulent activity using data analytics.
Discovers and follows up on fraud and crime. Produces evidence for law enforcement.
Audits outsourced financial and business processes to external service providers.
Reviews organization's current state before a formal audit. Focuses on control design, not operating effectiveness.

subtopics.real_life_scenario: A credit card company hires an external firm to assess whether their payment processing systems comply with PCI-DSS before the official certification audit. This is a Readiness Assessment.

subtopics.name: Control Self-Assessment (CSA)
subtopics.summary: A technique where management and staff assess their own internal controls — guided by an IS auditor acting as facilitator.
subtopics.primary_objective: Shift control monitoring responsibility to functional areas to reinforce management ownership of internal controls.
benefits: Increased employee awareness of organizational objectives
Increased communication between operational and top management
disadvantages: May be mistaken as a replacement for formal audit
Failure to act on suggestions damages morale
Lack of audit knowledge may limit effectiveness
subtopics.exam_tip: CSA's KEY benefit = management ownership of internal controls (not fraud detection or cost reduction).
subtopics.real_life_scenario: A manufacturing company conducts quarterly workshops where department managers assess their own procurement controls guided by the internal audit team. The IS auditor acts as facilitator, not as the one doing the testing.
subtopics.memory_aid: CSA = Control ownership by Staff and management. The Auditor Facilitates, not Audits.

subtopics.name: Integrated Auditing
subtopics.summary: Combines different audit disciplines (IT + financial + operational) to assess key internal controls with a focus on risk.
process: Identify organizational risk for the area being audited
Review and understand design of key controls
Test IT system support for key controls
Test operational effectiveness of management controls
Issue a combined report with findings
subtopics.benefit: One comprehensive audit report covering all audit disciplines.

topics.summary: Audit resources are deployed to areas representing the GREATEST risk. This requires understanding the organization, its environment, and conducting risk assessments.

subtopics.name: Individual Audit Assignments
planning_steps: Understand organization's mission, objectives, and processes
Understand governance structure related to audit objectives
Identify applicable policies, standards, and procedures
Identify opportunities for CAATs (Computer-Assisted Audit Techniques)

subtopics.name: Audit Risk and Materiality

types_of_audit_risk.Inherent Risk: Risk that exists WITHOUT considering controls. Exists because of the nature of the business.
types_of_audit_risk.Control Risk: Risk that a material error exists but WON'T be prevented or detected by internal controls.
types_of_audit_risk.Detection Risk: Risk that an IS auditor WON'T detect a material error during the audit.
types_of_audit_risk.Overall Audit Risk: Combination of inherent + control + detection risks.

subtopics.materiality: The relative significance of an issue in the context of the enterprise as a whole. Higher materiality = lower acceptable audit risk.
subtopics.real_life_scenario: An auditor reviewing a bank's trading systems knows trading carries HIGH inherent risk due to its complex nature. They design extensive testing to reduce detection risk.
subtopics.exam_tip: INHERENT risk = no controls considered. CONTROL risk = controls exist but may fail. DETECTION risk = auditor may miss it.
subtopics.memory_aid: I-C-D: Inherent → Control → Detection. Each one is the NEXT line of defense.

subtopics.name: Risk Assessment
subtopics.summary: Identifies, quantifies and prioritizes risk to guide management actions and audit planning.
subtopics.key_point: IT MANAGEMENT is responsible for conducting risk assessments. The IS auditor may assist but management owns the process.
subtopics.when_performed: Periodically and whenever significant changes occur (e.g., new system, new regulation, acquisition).

subtopics.name: Control Classifications

by_timing.Preventive Controls: Stop problems BEFORE they occur. Example: access restrictions, data validation.
by_timing.Detective Controls: IDENTIFY and report problems AS they occur. Example: audit logs, intrusion detection.
by_timing.Corrective Controls: MINIMIZE the impact and fix issues AFTER they occur. Example: data backups, disaster recovery.

by_nature.Manual Controls: Performed by people. Example: supervisor approval of transactions.
by_nature.Automated Controls: Performed by systems. Example: system-enforced password complexity.
by_nature.IT-Dependent Manual Controls: Manual controls relying on IT-generated reports. Example: manager reviews system-generated exception report.

subtopics.real_life_scenario: A bank's ATM: PIN requirement = Preventive. Transaction log = Detective. Backup files if system fails = Corrective.
subtopics.exam_tip: Daily data backup = CORRECTIVE control (restores after incident). It is NOT preventive.
subtopics.memory_aid: P-D-C: PREVENT the crime, DETECT the crime, CORRECT the damage.

subtopics.name: Control Relationship to Risk
subtopics.key_concept: Controls reduce risk. Auditors evaluate whether controls are adequately designed and operating effectively to mitigate identified risks.

subtopics.name: Audit Programs
subtopics.summary: A detailed set of audit procedures designed to achieve specific audit objectives within a given audit engagement.

subtopics.name: Agile Auditing
subtopics.summary: Applying agile project management principles to audits — shorter cycles, iterative feedback, flexible scope adjustments based on emerging findings.

subtopics.name: Compliance vs. Substantive Testing
subtopics.compliance_testing: Tests whether controls are OPERATING as designed. Example: Do users actually need manager approval for system access?
subtopics.substantive_testing: Tests whether the actual DATA and FINANCIAL information are accurate and complete.
subtopics.exam_tip: Compliance = test the control. Substantive = test the data/transaction.

subtopics.name: Sampling

types.Statistical Sampling: Uses probability theory — results can be projected to the population with a quantifiable confidence level.
types.Non-Statistical (Judgmental) Sampling: Based on auditor judgment — results cannot be statistically projected to the full population.

subtopics.sampling_risk: Risk that the sample does NOT represent the entire population accurately.

topics.key_concept: Evidence must be SUFFICIENT (enough), RELIABLE (trustworthy), RELEVANT (related to the finding), and USEFUL.

subtopics.name: Computer-Assisted Audit Techniques (CAATs)
subtopics.summary: Software tools used by IS auditors to directly access, analyze, and test data from IT systems.
subtopics.real_life_scenario: An auditor uses CAATs to analyze 100% of vendor payment transactions to detect duplicate payments — something impossible to do manually for large datasets.

subtopics.name: Continuous Auditing and Monitoring
subtopics.summary: Automated, ongoing monitoring of transactions and controls rather than periodic point-in-time audits.
subtopics.benefit: Detects anomalies in near real-time instead of months after the fact.

subtopics.name: Artificial Intelligence in IS Audit
subtopics.summary: AI and machine learning tools can analyze vast datasets, identify patterns, flag anomalies, and support audit decision-making.

key_concepts.Audit Report Structure: Executive summary, scope, objectives, findings, conclusions, recommendations, and management responses.
key_concepts.Follow-Up Activities: IS auditor must follow up to confirm management has implemented recommended corrective actions.
key_concepts.Audit Documentation: Work papers that support audit findings, conclusions, and evidence gathered.

topics.exam_tip: Audit reports should be timely, objective, clear, concise, constructive, and complete.

key_terminologies.IS Audit: Formal examination of information systems to verify compliance, security, and effectiveness.
key_terminologies.Audit Charter: Board-approved document defining the IS audit function's authority and scope.
key_terminologies.Inherent Risk: Risk present without controls being considered.
key_terminologies.Control Risk: Risk that controls fail to prevent or detect material errors.
key_terminologies.Detection Risk: Risk that auditors fail to detect existing errors.
key_terminologies.Materiality: The significance of an issue relative to the whole organization.
key_terminologies.CAATs: Computer-Assisted Audit Techniques — software tools for audit data analysis.
key_terminologies.CSA: Control Self-Assessment — management-led assessment of internal controls.
key_terminologies.ITAF: IT Assurance Framework — ISACA's comprehensive IS audit standards framework.
key_terminologies.Sampling Risk: Risk that a selected sample does not represent the full population.
key_terminologies.Compliance Testing: Tests whether controls operate as designed.
key_terminologies.Substantive Testing: Tests the accuracy and completeness of data/transactions.

domains.summary: This domain covers how organizations govern and manage their IT resources. It focuses on IT governance frameworks, risk management, data privacy, IT resource management, and performance monitoring.
domains.real_life_analogy: Think of IT governance like the board of directors of a company. They don't run daily operations but set direction, ensure accountability, and make sure IT serves the business strategy.

topics.topic_name: Organizational Structure, IT Governance and IT Strategy

subtopics.name: Enterprise Governance of Information and Technology (EGIT)
subtopics.summary: A framework ensuring IT activities align with and support business strategy and objectives.
subtopics.real_life_scenario: A hospital's IT department implements COBIT to align IT investments with patient care goals, ensuring electronic health records are secure, available, and compliant with regulations.

subtopics.name: Information Security Governance
subtopics.summary: A subset of overall IT governance focused on managing information security risks and ensuring the protection of information assets.

subtopics.name: Business Intelligence
subtopics.summary: Tools and technologies that analyze business data to support decision-making.

subtopics.name: Organizational Structure

key_roles.CIO: Manages IT strategy and IT department.
key_roles.IS Auditor: Provides independent assurance on IT controls and risks.

subtopics.segregation_of_duties: Critical control — no single person should control all stages of a key transaction.
subtopics.real_life_scenario: A bank clerk who enters a payment should NOT also be the one who approves it. Segregation of duties prevents fraud.
subtopics.memory_aid: SoD = Same person cannot DO and CHECK their own work.

topics.topic_name: IT Policies, Standards, Procedures and Guidelines

subtopics.name: Policies
subtopics.summary: High-level statements of management intent. WHAT the organization expects.
subtopics.example: The organization shall protect all sensitive customer data in accordance with applicable laws.
subtopics.key_point: Policies are MANDATORY. They are approved by senior management or the board.

subtopics.name: Standards
subtopics.summary: Specific requirements that support policies. HOW the organization meets policy intent.
subtopics.example: Passwords must be at least 12 characters with uppercase, numbers, and special characters.

subtopics.name: Procedures
subtopics.summary: Step-by-step instructions for implementing standards.
subtopics.example: Step 1: Go to account settings. Step 2: Click 'Change Password'. Step 3: Enter password meeting complexity requirements.

subtopics.name: Guidelines
subtopics.summary: Recommended practices — NOT mandatory. Provide flexibility.
subtopics.example: Users are encouraged to use password managers to manage their credentials.
subtopics.hierarchy_memory_aid: P-S-P-G: Policy → Standards → Procedures → Guidelines (from most mandatory to least mandatory)

topics.summary: A structured approach to identifying, assessing, and managing risk across the entire enterprise to achieve organizational objectives.

subtopics.name: Risk Management Life Cycle

phases.Risk Assessment: How likely is it? How bad would it be?
phases.Risk Response: What do we do about it? (Accept, Avoid, Transfer, Mitigate)

risk_responses.Accept: Acknowledge the risk and take no action (when impact is low).
risk_responses.Avoid: Eliminate the activity that creates the risk.
risk_responses.Transfer: Shift the risk to another party (e.g., insurance, outsourcing).
risk_responses.Mitigate: Implement controls to reduce the likelihood or impact.

subtopics.real_life_scenario: A retailer identifies the risk of a ransomware attack. They mitigate it with endpoint protection and daily backups, transfer some risk with cyber insurance, and accept the residual risk of a minor system downtime.
subtopics.memory_aid: ATMA: Accept, Transfer, Mitigate, Avoid — the 4 risk responses.

methods.Qualitative Risk Analysis: Uses descriptive ratings (High/Medium/Low). Based on judgment and experience. Faster but less precise.
methods.Quantitative Risk Analysis: Uses numerical values (e.g., Annual Loss Expectancy). More precise but requires more data and expertise.

quantitative_formulas.ALE: Annual Loss Expectancy = Single Loss Expectancy (SLE) × Annual Rate of Occurrence (ARO)
quantitative_formulas.SLE: Single Loss Expectancy = Asset Value × Exposure Factor
quantitative_formulas.example: Server worth $100,000, 30% chance of complete loss, occurs once a year. SLE = $30,000. ALE = $30,000.

topics.summary: Frameworks and controls to protect individuals' personal data in compliance with laws like GDPR.

subtopics.name: Data Inventory and Classification
subtopics.real_life_scenario: A hospital classifies patient health records as 'Restricted' — they require encryption at rest, strict access controls, and audit logging of every access.

subtopics.name: Data Subject Rights
rights: Right to Erasure (right to be forgotten)

subtopics.name: Human Resource Management

key_controls.Background Checks: Pre-employment screening to verify credentials and criminal history.
key_controls.Mandatory Leave / Job Rotation: Detects fraud by removing a person from their role temporarily.
key_controls.Separation of Duties: No single person controls all stages of a transaction.
key_controls.Termination Procedures: Immediate revocation of access when an employee leaves.

subtopics.real_life_scenario: A bank discovers accounting fraud during a mandatory 2-week vacation policy for financial staff. The relief employee flagged duplicate payment entries the original employee had hidden.
subtopics.exam_tip: Mandatory vacation and job rotation = detective controls for fraud.

subtopics.name: Enterprise Change Management
subtopics.summary: A formal process to control changes to IT systems to minimize unintended disruptions.
key_steps: Change approved by Change Advisory Board (CAB)
subtopics.real_life_scenario: An airline's IT team needs to update the reservation system. Without change management, a poorly tested update could crash bookings. Change management ensures it is tested, approved, and rolled back if it fails.

topics.topic_name: IT Service Management and Third-Party Governance

subtopics.name: Outsourcing Practices and Strategies
subtopics.real_life_scenario: A telecom company outsources its call center to a vendor in another country. The IS auditor verifies SLAs, data protection clauses, and performs periodic vendor audits to ensure customer data is protected.

subtopics.name: Cloud Governance

service_models.IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service): Customer manages OS, apps, and data. Provider manages hardware. Example: AWS EC2.
service_models.PaaS (Platform as a Service): Customer manages apps and data. Provider manages the platform. Example: Google App Engine.
service_models.SaaS (Software as a Service): Customer only manages data. Provider manages everything else. Example: Salesforce, Microsoft 365.

subtopics.exam_tip: In cloud models, the CUSTOMER still owns data privacy responsibility. The provider secures infrastructure but the customer configures security settings.

subtopics.name: Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)
subtopics.summary: Metrics that measure HOW WELL the organization is achieving its objectives.

subtopics.name: Key Risk Indicators (KRIs)
subtopics.summary: Metrics that signal INCREASING RISK before an issue occurs.
subtopics.example: Number of failed login attempts per day trending upward = early warning of brute force attack.

subtopics.name: Key Control Indicators (KCIs)
subtopics.summary: Metrics that measure the EFFECTIVENESS of specific controls.
subtopics.example: Percentage of patches applied within 30 days of release.

key_terminologies.COBIT: Control Objectives for Information Technologies — IT governance framework by ISACA.
key_terminologies.EGIT: Enterprise Governance of Information and Technology.
key_terminologies.SLA: Service Level Agreement — contractual commitment on service performance standards.
key_terminologies.ERM: Enterprise Risk Management — organization-wide risk management approach.
key_terminologies.ALE: Annual Loss Expectancy — quantitative measure of yearly risk impact.
key_terminologies.SLE: Single Loss Expectancy — loss from a single risk event.
key_terminologies.ARO: Annual Rate of Occurrence — how often a risk event is expected per year.
key_terminologies.SaaS / PaaS / IaaS: Cloud service models — Software/Platform/Infrastructure as a Service.
key_terminologies.KPI: Key Performance Indicator — measures goal achievement.
key_terminologies.KRI: Key Risk Indicator — early warning of increasing risk.
key_terminologies.KCI: Key Control Indicator — measures control effectiveness.
key_terminologies.Segregation of Duties (SoD): No single person controls all stages of a key process to prevent fraud.
key_terminologies.CAB: Change Advisory Board — approves changes to production IT systems.

domains.domain_name: Information Systems Acquisition, Development and Implementation
domains.summary: This domain covers how IT systems are planned, built, acquired, tested, and implemented. It focuses on project management, SDLC controls, application controls, testing methodologies, and change management.
domains.real_life_analogy: Think of building a new hospital. You need architects (project managers), building permits (governance), construction phases (SDLC), inspections at each phase, and a final walkthrough before opening. IS auditors inspect at every stage.

roles.Project Sponsor: Senior executive who champions the project and provides resources.
roles.Steering Committee: Provides oversight and direction for strategic projects.
roles.IS Auditor: Provides independent review at key project milestones.

techniques.Gantt Charts: Bar charts showing project schedule and task dependencies.
techniques.PERT (Program Evaluation and Review Tech: Analyzes time needed to complete tasks with uncertainty.
techniques.Critical Path Method (CPM): Identifies the longest sequence of tasks that determines project duration.

subtopics.name: SDLC Models

models.Waterfall: Sequential phases — each must complete before the next begins. Best for well-defined, stable requirements.
models.Prototyping: Build a working model early to gather feedback before full development.
models.Agile: Iterative sprints delivering working software frequently. Best for evolving requirements.
models.RAD (Rapid Application Development): Speed-focused development using prototypes and user feedback.
models.DevOps: Combines development and operations for continuous delivery with automation.

subtopics.exam_tip: Waterfall = best documented/controlled. Agile = most flexible. ISACA favors control and documentation.

subtopics.name: SDLC Phases

phases.description: Is the project technically and economically viable?
What does the system need to do?
How will the system be built?
phases.audit_focus: Security and control requirements built into design
Secure coding standards and code reviews

phases.description: Verifying the system works as designed.
phases.audit_focus: Test plans, test results, user acceptance testing (UAT)

phases.description: Going live with the new system.
phases.audit_focus: Migration controls, parallel running, rollback plans

phases.description: Confirming the system delivers expected benefits.
phases.audit_focus: Did the project achieve its objectives?

subtopics.real_life_scenario: A bank develops a new mobile banking app. IS auditors review security requirements in the design phase, check for SQL injection vulnerabilities in development, observe UAT testing, and review post-implementation performance metrics.

types.Input Controls: Ensure data entered is valid, complete, and accurate. Example: field validation, check digits.
types.Processing Controls: Ensure data is processed correctly. Example: run-to-run totals, batch controls.
types.Output Controls: Ensure output is complete, accurate, and delivered to authorized recipients.

topics.real_life_scenario: An e-commerce platform validates that a customer's credit card number passes Luhn Algorithm check before processing — this is an input control preventing invalid card numbers from entering the system.

types.Unit Testing: Testing individual code modules in isolation by developers.
types.System Testing: Testing the complete system against requirements.
types.User Acceptance Testing (UAT): Business users verify the system meets their needs.
types.Regression Testing: Ensuring new changes do not break existing functionality.
types.Penetration Testing: Simulated attacks to identify security vulnerabilities.

subtopics.name: System Implementation

strategies.Direct Cutover (Big Bang): Switch from old to new system immediately. Highest risk.
strategies.Parallel Running: Run old and new systems simultaneously. Safest but most costly.
strategies.Phased Implementation: Implement in stages by location or function.
strategies.Pilot Implementation: Deploy to a limited group first to test before full rollout.

subtopics.exam_tip: Parallel running = SAFEST strategy. Direct cutover = HIGHEST risk but lowest cost.

topics.summary: After a system goes live, an IS auditor evaluates whether it delivers expected benefits, controls are effective, and lessons learned are captured.
key_questions: Did the project stay within budget and timeline?
Are the controls operating as designed?
Did the system achieve the planned business benefits?

key_terminologies.SDLC: System Development Life Cycle — structured process for building IT systems.
key_terminologies.UAT: User Acceptance Testing — final testing by business users.
key_terminologies.Agile: Iterative development methodology delivering working software in short sprints.
key_terminologies.DevOps: Practice combining development and operations for continuous integration and delivery.
key_terminologies.Parallel Running: Simultaneously running old and new systems to ensure accuracy.
key_terminologies.Regression Testing: Testing to ensure new changes don't break existing functionality.
key_terminologies.Penetration Testing: Authorized simulated attack to find security vulnerabilities.
key_terminologies.Input Controls: Controls ensuring accuracy and completeness of data entered into a system.
key_terminologies.Feasibility Study: Analysis of whether a proposed project is viable.

domains.domain_name: Information Systems Operations and Business Resilience
domains.summary: This domain covers the management and monitoring of IT operations, infrastructure, and ensuring systems remain available and can recover from disruptions. It includes IT asset management, incident and problem management, database management, business continuity, and disaster recovery.
domains.real_life_analogy: Think of a city's emergency services. Police, fire, and ambulance services run daily operations, but the city also has emergency protocols when disaster strikes — evacuation routes, backup hospitals, and communication plans. This domain covers both normal operations AND emergency preparedness for IT.

key_concepts.OSI Model: 7-layer model for network communication: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.
key_concepts.TCP/IP: Core communication protocol of the internet.
key_concepts.DNS (Domain Name System): Translates domain names to IP addresses.

subtopics.name: The OSI Model
subtopics.summary: The Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model is a 7-layer framework that describes how data moves across a network — from the physical wires at the bottom to the application a person actually uses at the top. Each layer has one job and interacts only with the layers directly above and below it.

subtopics.discussion:
Think of sending a physical letter. You write the message (the application's job), put it in an envelope and seal it (formatting and encryption), the postal service picks the route between cities (addressing), decides registered mail or a postcard (reliable vs fast delivery), and finally roads and trucks physically move it (the wires). The OSI model splits network communication the same way — into seven stages, each responsible for one part of the journey, each able to do its job without knowing the details of the others.
As data travels down the stack on the sending device, every layer adds its own header — this is called encapsulation. The receiving device reverses it, stripping one header per layer on the way up. That is why the same data is called a Segment at Layer 4, a Packet at Layer 3, and a Frame at Layer 2.
Why auditors care: the model gives you a shared vocabulary for WHERE a control or a weakness lives. A firewall rule that blocks ports is a Layer 4 (Transport) control. An IPsec VPN that encrypts traffic is a Layer 3 control. Phishing that tricks a user is a Layer 7 (Application) problem — no network control below it will stop it. When you can name the layer, you can reason about whether a control is placed where the risk actually is.

layers.technical: Where network-aware programs operate and provide services to the user.
layers.analogy: The message itself — what you actually wrote in the letter.
layers.protocols: HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, DNS, SNMP, SSH
layers.devices: End-user applications — web browsers, email clients, API clients

layers.technical: Translates, encrypts, and compresses data so both ends interpret it the same way.
layers.analogy: Translating the letter into a language the recipient reads, and sealing the envelope.

layers.technical: Opens, manages, and terminates the ongoing conversation between two systems.
layers.analogy: Agreeing to start talking, taking turns, and saying goodbye at the end.

layers.technical: Provides end-to-end delivery, reliability, flow control, and error recovery. Port numbers identify the service.
layers.analogy: Choosing registered mail (TCP) versus a postcard (UDP), and numbering the pages.

layers.technical: Handles logical addressing and routes packets across separate networks.
layers.analogy: The postal service deciding which cities the letter passes through.
layers.protocols: IP (IPv4/IPv6), ICMP, IPsec, IGMP, OSPF, BGP

layers.technical: Provides node-to-node delivery, framing, MAC addressing, and error detection.
layers.analogy: The local delivery van carrying the letter from one depot to the next.

layers.technical: Transmits raw bits over the physical medium — electrical, optical, or radio.
layers.analogy: The roads and the physical movement of the envelope itself.
layers.protocols: Ethernet physical media, fiber, DSL, 802.11 radio (PHY)

subtopics.real_life_scenario: An IS auditor reviews a breach where attackers read login credentials off the corporate Wi-Fi. The network team insists the firewall (Layer 4) and router ACLs (Layer 3) were correctly configured — and they were. The real gap was at Layer 2: the wireless network used an outdated encryption standard, so traffic between laptops and the access point could be captured from the air. Naming the layer pinpointed the fix — upgrade the Layer 2 wireless encryption — instead of re-auditing controls that were never the problem.
common_mistakes: Confusing Layer 2 (Data Link — MAC addresses, switches) with Layer 3 (Network — IP addresses, routers). This is a frequent exam trap.
Assuming a firewall protects every layer. A traditional port-based firewall works at Layer 4 and cannot stop a Layer 7 attack such as phishing or SQL injection.
Thinking encryption lives in only one layer. It can sit at Layer 6 (TLS), Layer 3 (IPsec VPN), or Layer 2 (Wi-Fi) — and the layer decides what the encryption actually protects.
Memorizing the layer names but not what each layer does. The exam tests whether you can place a control or a symptom at the right layer, not recall the list.
subtopics.memory_aid: Bottom-up (Layer 1→7): 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away' — Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. Top-down: 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing'.
subtopics.exam_tip: When a question describes a symptom, identify the layer first. 'Cannot reach any website, but the connection is up' points to Layer 7 (DNS). 'Intermittent drops on one desk' often points to Layer 1 (physical cabling). Naming the layer narrows the answer fast.

subtopics.name: Capacity Management
subtopics.summary: Ensuring IT resources (storage, processing power, network bandwidth) are sufficient to meet current and future demand.
subtopics.real_life_scenario: An e-commerce site plans for 10x normal traffic on Black Friday. Without capacity management, the site crashes under peak load, losing millions in sales.

subtopics.name: Process of Incident Handling

incident_vs_problem.Incident: An unplanned interruption to an IT service. Example: website is down.
incident_vs_problem.Problem: The underlying ROOT CAUSE of one or more incidents. Example: faulty network switch causing repeated outages.

subtopics.real_life_scenario: A company's email server is unresponsive (Incident). Technicians restore it quickly. Later, the Problem Management team investigates and discovers a memory leak in the email server software — the root cause (Problem). They then patch the software permanently.
subtopics.memory_aid: INCIDENT = what happened now. PROBLEM = WHY it keeps happening.

topics.topic_name: IT Change, Configuration and Patch Management

subtopics.name: Patch Management
subtopics.summary: Regular updates to software to fix known security vulnerabilities.
subtopics.exam_tip: Unpatched systems are a HIGH RISK finding. Patch management is a preventive control.
subtopics.real_life_scenario: The WannaCry ransomware attack in 2017 exploited a Windows vulnerability that had a patch available for 2 months prior. Organizations that had not applied the patch were devastated.

subtopics.name: Release Management
subtopics.summary: Controlled process for moving software changes from development to production environments.

subtopics.name: IS Operations
key_controls: Separation of duties between developers and production systems

topics.summary: Collecting, storing, monitoring, and analyzing logs generated by IT systems.
key_controls: Log integrity — logs should not be modifiable by regular users
Log retention — how long logs are kept
Log review — regular monitoring for anomalies
Centralized logging — SIEM (Security Information and Event Management)
topics.real_life_scenario: During a forensic investigation, security analysts use firewall and server logs to trace a data breach back to the exact time, source IP, and accounts accessed — all captured in the audit trail.
topics.exam_tip: Logs are DETECTIVE controls. They don't prevent incidents but provide evidence and enable detection.

subtopics.name: DBMS Architecture
subtopics.summary: Database Management System (DBMS) manages databases and controls access to data.

types.Relational (RDBMS): Tables with relationships. Example: Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL.
types.NoSQL: Non-relational. Example: MongoDB, Cassandra. Used for unstructured data.

subtopics.name: Database Controls
controls: Database access controls — only authorized users access data
Data encryption — data at rest and in transit
Audit trails — log all database access and changes
Backup and recovery — regular database backups
subtopics.real_life_scenario: A hospital's patient database has role-based access — doctors see clinical records, billing staff see financial records, and no one can access both. The DBA (Database Administrator) has full access but is separated from clinical operations.

topics.summary: A process to identify and evaluate the potential effects of disruption to critical business operations.
outputs: Critical processes ranked by business impact

key_metrics.RTO (Recovery Time Objective): HOW FAST must we recover after a disruption? (Maximum acceptable downtime)
key_metrics.RPO (Recovery Point Objective): HOW MUCH DATA can we afford to lose? (Maximum acceptable data loss)
key_metrics.MTD (Maximum Tolerable Downtime): The LONGEST an organization can survive without a specific function.

topics.real_life_scenario: A bank identifies that online banking is critical and sets RTO = 4 hours (system must be restored within 4 hours) and RPO = 15 minutes (no more than 15 minutes of transaction data can be lost). This determines backup frequency and recovery site requirements.

RTO.analogy: How long the store is closed

RPO.analogy: How old the last backup is

topics.exam_tip: RTO = time. RPO = data. Lower RTO and RPO = more expensive recovery infrastructure.
topics.memory_aid: RTO = 'Return To Operations'. RPO = 'Recovery Point (data) Objective'.

backup_schemes.Full Backup: Complete copy of all data. Slowest to complete, fastest to restore.
backup_schemes.Incremental Backup: Only data changed since LAST BACKUP. Fastest to complete, slowest to restore.
backup_schemes.Differential Backup: Only data changed since LAST FULL BACKUP. Compromise between full and incremental.

topics.3-2-1 Backup Rule: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite.
topics.exam_tip: Incremental = smallest backup size. Full = quickest restore. Differential = middle ground.

topics.summary: A plan ensuring critical business functions can continue during and after a major disruption.

subtopics.name: IT Business Continuity Planning
subtopics.scope: Broader than DRP — covers people, processes, facilities, and technology. BCP is the UMBRELLA plan.

drp_vs_bcp.BCP: Broader — covers entire business operations during a disruption.
drp_vs_bcp.DRP (Disaster Recovery Plan): Narrower — focuses specifically on restoring IT systems and data.

subtopics.memory_aid: BCP = Business keeps CONTINUING. DRP = Data and systems Recovering. BCP contains DRP.

subtopics.name: Business Continuity Planning Process
steps: Initiation — management commitment and scope definition

testing_types.Checklist Review: Team reviews BCP document for completeness — least thorough.
testing_types.Walkthrough/Tabletop Exercise: Team verbally walks through the plan — no actual systems involved.
testing_types.Simulation Test: A hypothetical scenario is presented and teams respond — no real systems activated.
testing_types.Parallel Test: Backup systems are activated and tested while primary systems remain operational.
testing_types.Full Interruption Test: Primary systems are actually shut down — most thorough but highest risk.

subtopics.real_life_scenario: A financial firm conducts a full interruption test on a Sunday where they actually switch to their disaster recovery site to verify it can handle real transaction loads — the most thorough but riskiest test type.
subtopics.exam_tip: Full interruption test = MOST thorough. Checklist review = LEAST thorough. IS auditors prefer more comprehensive tests.

recovery_sites.Hot Site: Fully equipped and operational. Can take over within HOURS. Most expensive.
recovery_sites.Warm Site: Partially equipped. Needs hours to days to become operational. Moderate cost.
recovery_sites.Cold Site: Basic infrastructure only (power, connectivity). Takes days to weeks. Cheapest.
recovery_sites.Mobile Site: Portable recovery unit that can be deployed anywhere.
recovery_sites.Reciprocal Agreement: Two organizations agree to use each other's facilities in a disaster — lowest cost, least reliable.

topics.real_life_scenario: A bank has a hot site 50km away that mirrors all transactions in real-time. When an earthquake damages their primary data center, operations continue from the hot site within 2 hours.
topics.memory_aid: Hot = Hottest (fastest, most expensive). Cold = Coldest (slowest, cheapest).

key_terminologies.RTO: Recovery Time Objective — maximum acceptable system downtime.
key_terminologies.RPO: Recovery Point Objective — maximum acceptable data loss.
key_terminologies.MTD: Maximum Tolerable Downtime — longest the business can survive without a function.
key_terminologies.BCP: Business Continuity Plan — keeps business running during disruptions.
key_terminologies.DRP: Disaster Recovery Plan — restores IT systems after a disruption.
key_terminologies.BIA: Business Impact Analysis — evaluates impact of disruptions on critical processes.
key_terminologies.Hot Site: Fully equipped backup facility that can be operational within hours.
key_terminologies.Cold Site: Basic backup facility requiring days/weeks to become operational.
key_terminologies.SIEM: Security Information and Event Management — centralized log monitoring and analysis.
key_terminologies.DBMS: Database Management System — software managing database access and storage.
key_terminologies.Patch Management: Process of applying security updates to software systems.
key_terminologies.Incident: An unplanned interruption to an IT service.
key_terminologies.Problem: The root cause of one or more incidents.
key_terminologies.Incremental Backup: Backs up only data changed since the last backup.
key_terminologies.Differential Backup: Backs up data changed since the last FULL backup.

domains.summary: The LARGEST domain. Covers how organizations protect their information assets through security policies, physical and logical access controls, cryptography, network security, data loss prevention, cloud security, and threat management. This is where cybersecurity meets audit.
domains.real_life_analogy: Think of an airport security system. There are physical barriers (fences, secured doors), identity checks (passports, boarding passes), scanning technology (X-ray, metal detectors), monitoring (cameras, staff), and protocols for when something goes wrong. This domain is the 'airport security' for IT systems.

topics.topic_name: Information Asset Security Policies, Frameworks, Standards and Guidelines

subtopics.name: Information Security Frameworks and Standards

frameworks.ISO/IEC 27001: International standard for Information Security Management Systems (ISMS). Provides requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving an ISMS.
frameworks.NIST Cybersecurity Framework: Five core functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
frameworks.COBIT 2019: IT governance and management framework including security controls.
frameworks.PCI-DSS: Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard — required for organizations handling credit card data.
frameworks.GDPR: General Data Protection Regulation — EU law protecting personal data of EU residents.

subtopics.exam_tip: ISO 27001 = certification-based security standard. NIST CSF = voluntary framework. PCI-DSS = required for card payment industry.

subtopics.name: Information Security Baselines
subtopics.summary: Minimum security requirements that all systems must meet.
subtopics.example: All servers must have the latest patches installed, antivirus running, and unnecessary services disabled.

subtopics.name: Environmental Exposures and Controls

threats_and_controls.Fire: Fire suppression systems (FM-200 for data centers), smoke detectors, fire extinguishers.
threats_and_controls.Flooding: Raised flooring, water sensors, locate data centers away from flood zones.
threats_and_controls.Power Failure: UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) for immediate backup, generators for extended outages.
threats_and_controls.Temperature: Precision air conditioning in server rooms, temperature monitoring alerts.

subtopics.real_life_scenario: A data center uses raised flooring, water leak detectors under the floor, FM-200 gas suppression (safe for electronics), and redundant UPS systems to protect against environmental threats.

subtopics.name: Physical Access Exposures and Controls

controls.Mantrap (Airlock): Two-door controlled entry — a person enters the first door, is authenticated, then the second door opens. Prevents tailgating.
controls.Biometric Access: Fingerprint, iris scan, facial recognition — something you ARE.
controls.Badge/Keycard Access: Something you HAVE — provides audit trail of entry/exit.
controls.CCTV: 24/7 monitoring and recording of facility access.
controls.Security Guards: Human monitoring, verification, and response capability.
controls.Clean Desk Policy: No sensitive documents left visible when workstations are unattended.

subtopics.real_life_scenario: A bank's data center requires badge scan + PIN entry at the perimeter, biometric scan at the server room door, and all entry/exits are logged and reviewed weekly by security.
subtopics.exam_tip: Mantrap = most effective physical control against tailgating/piggybacking.

topics.summary: Ensuring the RIGHT people have the RIGHT access to the RIGHT resources at the RIGHT time.

subtopics.name: Authentication, Authorization and Accountability (AAA)

definitions.Authentication: Verifying WHO you are. Example: username + password, biometrics.
definitions.Authorization: Determining WHAT you can do after authentication. Example: role-based access.
definitions.Accountability: Tracking WHAT you did. Example: audit logs of actions taken.

authentication_factors.Something You Have: Smart card, hardware token, mobile phone (OTP).

subtopics.MFA: Multi-Factor Authentication — using 2 or more different factor types. Strongest authentication.
subtopics.real_life_scenario: Online banking requires your password (something you know) AND a one-time code sent to your phone (something you have). This is MFA — even if your password is stolen, the attacker cannot log in.
subtopics.exam_tip: The three A's in order: Authenticate (who), Authorize (what you may do), Account (what you did). MFA = factors from DIFFERENT categories. Shared accounts destroy accountability.
subtopics.summary: Identity and access management rests on three questions — the three A's. Authentication proves WHO you are, Authorization decides WHAT you may do, and Accountability records WHAT you did.

illustration.caption: The three A's in order. You must be authenticated before you can be authorized, and accountability is only meaningful when authentication reliably ties an action to one person.

subtopics.discussion:
Every access decision answers three questions in sequence. Authentication establishes identity — it proves you are who you claim. Authorization then decides what that identity is permitted to do. Accountability records what was actually done, so actions can be traced back to a person.
The order matters: you cannot authorize someone who has not been authenticated, and accountability collapses if authentication is weak. If several people share one login, the logs can show what the account did but not which person did it — so the account, not a person, is accountable. That is exactly why shared or generic accounts are a recurring audit finding.
Authentication strength comes from factors, grouped into three categories: something you know (a password or PIN), something you have (a token or phone), and something you are (a fingerprint or face). Multi-factor authentication (MFA) combines factors from DIFFERENT categories. Two passwords are not MFA — both are 'something you know', so an attacker who phishes one technique gets both. A password plus a phone code is true MFA, because stealing the password alone is not enough.
For an auditor: weak or shared authentication undermines the entire chain — without trustworthy authentication, neither authorization nor accountability can be relied upon.
common_mistakes: Confusing authentication with authorization. Authentication proves identity; authorization grants permissions. A correctly authenticated user can still be denied access to a resource.
Thinking two passwords is multi-factor. MFA needs factors from DIFFERENT categories (know / have / are). Two things you know is single-factor — two-step, not multi-factor.
Forgetting that accountability depends on authentication. With shared or generic accounts the logs cannot attribute an action to a person, so accountability is lost — a standard audit finding.

subtopics.name: Zero-Trust Architecture
subtopics.principle: NEVER TRUST, ALWAYS VERIFY — even users inside the network must be continuously authenticated and authorized.
subtopics.contrast: Traditional security = trust inside the perimeter. Zero-trust = trust nothing inside or outside by default.
subtopics.real_life_scenario: A company implements Zero Trust where every employee must authenticate to access each application, even from inside the corporate office. Lateral movement by attackers is blocked because they cannot freely access other systems even after breaching one.
subtopics.summary: Zero Trust is a security model built on one principle — never trust, always verify. No request is trusted because of where it comes from; every access is authenticated and authorized, every time, inside the network as much as outside.

subtopics.discussion:
The traditional security model works like a castle and moat: build one strong perimeter, and treat everything inside it as trusted. Its fatal weakness is what happens after a breach — an attacker who gets through the wall, by phishing one employee or compromising one server, is now 'inside' and trusted, free to move sideways from system to system. This is called lateral movement.
Zero Trust removes the idea of a trusted inside. Its principle is never trust, always verify: every access request is authenticated and authorized on its own merits, no matter where it originates. Being on the corporate network grants nothing. A request from a desk in head office is checked exactly like a request from the public internet.
Zero Trust is not a product you buy — it is an architecture made of several controls working together: strong identity verification, device-posture checks, least-privilege access, network microsegmentation, and continuous monitoring with an 'assume breach' mindset.
For an auditor: the value of Zero Trust is containment. It does not promise to stop every breach, but by verifying every step it stops a single compromised system from becoming a compromise of the whole network.
common_mistakes: Thinking Zero Trust means 'no trust at all' or 'no access'. It means no IMPLICIT trust — access is still granted, but only after explicit verification, every time.
Believing Zero Trust is a single product. It is an architecture — identity verification, device posture, least privilege, segmentation, and monitoring working together.
Assuming the corporate network is a safe zone. Under Zero Trust, location on the network grants no trust — an internal request is verified exactly like an external one.
subtopics.exam_tip: Zero Trust = never trust, always verify. Network location grants NO trust. Its main benefit is blocking an attacker's lateral movement after an initial breach.

subtopics.name: Privileged Access Management (PAM)
subtopics.summary: Privileged Access Management (PAM) is the set of controls for administrator, root, and service accounts — the accounts powerful enough to change configurations, bypass controls, and erase their own tracks.
controls: Just-in-time access — privileged access only when needed
Session recording — all privileged sessions logged and monitored
Password vaulting — privileged credentials stored in secure vault
Dual control — two people required to access critical admin functions
subtopics.exam_tip: Privileged accounts are the highest risk. PAM = vaulting, just-in-time access, session recording, approval/dual control, least privilege. Minimize standing access and review the recordings.

subtopics.discussion:
Privileged accounts — administrator, root, domain admin, and service accounts — are the highest-value target in any environment. Their power is the problem: a privileged account can disable security controls, read or change any data, create new accounts, and delete the very logs that would record the abuse. A breach of one ordinary account is contained; a breach of a privileged account can mean the whole environment.
PAM reduces that risk with a layered set of controls. Credential vaulting stores privileged passwords in a secure vault rather than in people's heads or scripts. Just-in-time (JIT) access replaces always-on admin rights with short, task-scoped grants that expire automatically — so the account is not a standing target. Session recording captures everything done in a privileged session. Approval and dual control require a second person to authorize the most sensitive actions. Underpinning all of it is least privilege: grant the minimum rights needed, for the minimum time.
For an auditor: two checks matter most. First, that privileged access is minimized and time-bound rather than permanent. Second, that session recordings are actually reviewed — an unwatched recording deters nothing and detects nothing. The review is the control.
common_mistakes: Treating privileged accounts like normal accounts. Admin and root accounts can disable controls and erase their own tracks — they need vaulting, monitoring, and minimization that ordinary accounts do not.
Leaving privileged access standing permanently. Modern PAM grants access just-in-time — for a defined task and time window — so the account is not a constant target.
Recording privileged sessions but never reviewing them. An unmonitored recording deters nothing and detects nothing; the review is the control.

subtopics.name: Types of Access Controls

types.DAC (Discretionary Access Control): Data owner decides who gets access. Most flexible, least secure. Example: file sharing permissions in Windows.
types.MAC (Mandatory Access Control): System-enforced based on classification labels. Most secure, least flexible. Used in military/government.
types.RBAC (Role-Based Access Control): Access based on job role. Most common in enterprises. Example: all managers can approve invoices.
types.ABAC (Attribute-Based Access Control): Access based on multiple attributes (role + location + time + device). Most granular control.

subtopics.exam_tip: Tell the models apart by who decides: DAC = the data owner; MAC = the system (labels); RBAC = your job role; ABAC = multiple attributes. RBAC is most common in business; MAC is most secure.
subtopics.memory_aid: D-M-R-A: Discretionary → Mandatory → Role-Based → Attribute-Based (least to most control).
subtopics.summary: Access control models differ in one thing — who decides who gets access. DAC leaves it to the data owner, MAC to the system, RBAC to your job role, and ABAC to a combination of attributes.

subtopics.discussion:
An access control model is the rule for deciding who may do what. Four models appear on the exam, and the cleanest way to tell them apart is to ask who makes the decision.
Under Discretionary Access Control (DAC), the data owner decides — they grant and revoke access at their discretion, the way file-sharing permissions work. It is flexible but the least secure, because decisions are scattered across many owners.
Under Mandatory Access Control (MAC), the system enforces access from classification labels — Top Secret, Secret, Confidential — and an owner cannot override the policy. It is the most secure and the most rigid, which is why it is used in military and government settings.
Under Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), access follows your job role: all managers can approve invoices, all clerks can enter them. RBAC is the most common model in business because it scales — you manage a handful of roles instead of thousands of individual grants.
Under Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC), the decision uses multiple attributes at once — role plus device, location, time of day, sensitivity. It is the most granular and context-aware, and underpins Zero Trust architectures.
For an auditor: 'most secure' is not the same as 'best'. MAC is the most secure but most enterprises rightly choose RBAC, because the right model is the one that fits the environment's risk and manageability.
common_mistakes: Confusing DAC and MAC. In DAC the data OWNER decides who gets access; in MAC the SYSTEM enforces access from classification labels and the owner cannot override it.
Thinking RBAC and ABAC are the same. RBAC decides on job role alone; ABAC decides on multiple attributes — role plus context such as device, location, and time.

Assuming 'most secure' means 'best choice'. MAC is the most rigid and secure, but most enterprises use RBAC because it balances security with manageability — the right model depends on the environment.

subtopics.name: Firewalls
subtopics.summary: Security devices that control network traffic based on defined rules.

types.Packet Filtering Firewall: Inspects packet headers (IP, port). Basic — does not inspect content.
types.Stateful Inspection Firewall: Tracks connection state. More intelligent than packet filtering.
types.Application Layer Firewall (Proxy): Inspects application content. Can detect application-level attacks.
types.Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW): Combines traditional firewall with DPI, IPS, and application awareness.

subtopics.real_life_scenario: A company's NGFW blocks an employee from accessing a known malware-hosting website, even though the HTTPS connection looks legitimate, because it analyzes the destination's reputation and SSL certificate.

subtopics.name: Unified Threat Management (UTM)
subtopics.summary: A single device combining multiple security functions: firewall, IDS/IPS, antivirus, VPN, web filtering.

subtopics.name: Network Segmentation
subtopics.summary: Dividing a network into isolated segments to contain breaches and limit lateral movement.
subtopics.example: Separating the HR network from the production server network. If HR is breached, attackers cannot reach servers.
subtopics.dmz: Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) — a network segment between internal trusted network and untrusted internet. Web servers typically placed here.
subtopics.real_life_scenario: A retailer separates customer Wi-Fi from the POS (Point of Sale) network. A malware-infected customer device cannot reach the payment system.

subtopics.name: Endpoint Security
subtopics.exam_tip: Endpoint = any device connecting to the network (laptop, phone, tablet, server). Each endpoint is a potential attack vector.

topics.summary: Technologies and processes that detect and prevent unauthorized transfer of sensitive data outside the organization.

data_states.Data at Rest: Stored data (databases, files). Controls: encryption, access controls.
data_states.Data in Motion: Data being transmitted over a network. Controls: TLS/SSL encryption, DLP network sensors.
data_states.Data in Use: Data being actively processed. Controls: screen watermarks, copy-paste restrictions.

topics.real_life_scenario: A financial firm's DLP system detects an employee trying to email a spreadsheet containing 500 credit card numbers to their personal Gmail. The email is blocked and a security alert is generated.
topics.exam_tip: DLP's purpose = PREVENT unauthorized data exfiltration. It is a detective AND preventive control.

subtopics.discussion:
Symmetric encryption is the oldest and fastest form of encryption. One key locks the data and the very same key unlocks it. Because it is fast, symmetric encryption does the heavy lifting in the real world — it encrypts the actual files, disk volumes, database contents, and the bulk of network traffic.
The catch is key distribution. Before two parties can communicate, they must both already hold the same secret key. If an attacker intercepts that key while it is being shared, every message protected by it is exposed — the algorithm was never the weak point, the hand-off was. This 'how do we share the key safely?' problem is exactly what asymmetric encryption was invented to solve.
That is why modern systems use both: asymmetric encryption to safely exchange a symmetric key, then fast symmetric encryption for the actual data. This is called a hybrid approach, and HTTPS works this way every time you load a secure web page. For an auditor: AES is the current symmetric standard; DES is broken and 3DES is deprecated — finding a system still relying on DES is a legitimate audit finding.
examples: DES — broken, must not be used
subtopics.analogy: A house key — the same key locks and unlocks the door. The hard part is not the lock; it is handing a copy of the key to someone else without anyone copying it on the way.
common_mistakes: Thinking symmetric encryption is weak because it is 'old'. AES is symmetric and is the modern gold standard — the weakness is key distribution, not the algorithm.
Confusing the key-distribution problem with an algorithm weakness. The symmetric algorithm is strong; getting the shared key to both parties securely is the hard part.
Assuming symmetric and asymmetric compete. Real systems use both — asymmetric to exchange the key, symmetric for the data itself.
subtopics.exam_tip: Symmetric = ONE shared key, fast, used for bulk data. AES is the current standard; DES is broken and 3DES is deprecated. If a question stresses speed or encrypting large volumes of data, the answer is symmetric.

subtopics.how_it_works: Data encrypted with the PUBLIC key can only be decrypted with the matching PRIVATE key. The two keys are generated together as a mathematically linked pair; knowing the public key does not let anyone work out the private key.
subtopics.discussion:
Asymmetric encryption solved the problem symmetric encryption could not: how to communicate securely with someone you have never met and never shared a secret with. Each person generates a key pair — a public key they publish freely, and a private key they never share. The two are mathematically bound, but the maths only runs one way: you cannot derive the private key from the public key.
The direction of the keys depends on the goal. For CONFIDENTIALITY, the sender encrypts with the recipient's PUBLIC key, and only the recipient's PRIVATE key can open it. For a DIGITAL SIGNATURE the roles reverse — the sender signs with their OWN private key, and anyone can verify with the sender's public key. Mixing up these two directions is the most common asymmetric-cryptography mistake.
Asymmetric encryption is slow because it relies on heavy mathematics, so it is never used for bulk data. Instead it does small, high-value jobs: exchanging a symmetric key, signing, and authenticating. RSA is the long-established algorithm; ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) achieves the same strength with much shorter keys, which is why mobile and IoT devices prefer it.
examples: ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) — same strength, shorter keys
subtopics.analogy: A public mailbox — anyone can drop a letter in through the slot (encrypt with the public key), but only the owner has the key to open the box and read it (the private key).
use_cases: Key exchange (delivering a symmetric key safely)
common_mistakes: Mixing up which key does what. For CONFIDENTIALITY: encrypt with the recipient's PUBLIC key, decrypt with their PRIVATE key. For a DIGITAL SIGNATURE the roles reverse: sign with the sender's PRIVATE key, verify with the sender's PUBLIC key.
Thinking asymmetric replaces symmetric. It is far too slow for bulk data; it is used to exchange keys and to sign — symmetric still encrypts the actual data.
Believing the public key must be protected. The public key is meant to be public — sharing it widely is the point. Only the private key is secret, and leaking it is catastrophic.
subtopics.exam_tip: Asymmetric = a public + private key PAIR, slower, used for key exchange and digital signatures. Most real systems are hybrid: asymmetric exchanges the key, symmetric encrypts the data.

subtopics.how_it_works: Signing: the sender runs the message through a hash function to get a fixed-length digest, then encrypts that digest with their PRIVATE key — the result is the signature. Verifying: the receiver decrypts the signature with the sender's PUBLIC key to recover the original digest, independently hashes the received message, and compares the two digests. If they match, the message is authentic and unaltered.
subtopics.discussion:
A digital signature answers three questions at once: did this really come from who it claims, has it been changed, and can the sender later deny it. It works by combining hashing with asymmetric cryptography.
First the message is hashed — reduced to a short fixed-length digest that changes completely if even one character of the message changes. The sender then encrypts that digest with their own private key. Because only the sender holds that private key, only they could have produced a signature that opens with their public key — that is the proof of identity.
To verify, the receiver does two things in parallel: decrypt the signature with the sender's public key to recover the original digest, and separately hash the received message to compute a fresh digest. If the two digests are identical, the message is authentic (it came from the holder of the private key) and intact (it has not been altered since signing). If even one byte changed in transit, the fresh hash will not match and verification fails.
The critical limit: a digital signature does NOT provide confidentiality. The message itself is not hidden — anyone can still read it. Signing proves origin and integrity; if the content must also be secret, it has to be encrypted separately.
provides: Integrity — proves the message was not altered
Non-repudiation — the sender cannot later deny sending it
subtopics.real_life_scenario: A CEO digitally signs a PDF contract. The recipient verifies the signature with the CEO's public certificate — confirming the document genuinely came from the CEO and has not been altered since signing. If the CEO later claims they never approved it, the valid signature is the evidence that they did: non-repudiation.
common_mistakes: Thinking a digital signature hides or encrypts the message. It does NOT provide confidentiality — it proves origin and integrity. Anyone can still read the message unless it is separately encrypted.
Reversing the keys. The sender signs with their PRIVATE key; verifiers check with the sender's PUBLIC key. (Encrypting for confidentiality runs in the opposite direction.)
Confusing a digital signature with an electronic signature. A typed name or a scanned image of a signature is not cryptographic — only a digital signature provides integrity and non-repudiation.
subtopics.memory_aid: Sign with what is PRIVATE to you; everyone else verifies with what is PUBLIC. Integrity comes from the hash; identity comes from the private key.
subtopics.exam_tip: Digital signature = sign with the sender's PRIVATE key, verify with the sender's PUBLIC key. It provides authentication, integrity, and non-repudiation — but NOT confidentiality.

subtopics.discussion:
Asymmetric cryptography only works if you can trust that a public key really belongs to the party you think it does. On its own, a public key is just a number — an attacker could hand you their key while claiming to be your bank. PKI solves this with a trusted third party.
A Certificate Authority (CA) is an organisation everyone agrees to trust. It verifies an identity and then issues a digital certificate — a document that binds a public key to that identity and is signed by the CA's own private key. Because your software already trusts the CA, and the CA vouches for the certificate, you can now trust the public key inside it.
CAs are arranged in a hierarchy called the chain of trust. At the top sits the root CA — self-signed, and so important it is usually kept physically offline. The root signs intermediate CAs, which in turn sign the everyday end-entity certificates used by websites, people, and devices. Trust delegates downward; a verifier checks a certificate by chaining upward, link by link, until it reaches a root it already trusts.
For an auditor: protecting the root CA's private key is the single most important control in the whole system — if it is compromised, every certificate beneath it is worthless. Auditors check that the root is kept offline, that issuance follows the documented Certificate Policy, and that the Registration Authority properly verifies identity before any certificate is issued.

components.role: Issues and digitally signs certificates. The trusted party that everyone relies on.
components.analogy: A passport office — a trusted authority whose stamp others accept.

components.role: Verifies the identity of a requester before the CA will issue a certificate.
components.analogy: The clerk who checks your documents before the passport is printed.

components.role: Binds a public key to an identity and is signed by the CA. Holds the subject, public key, validity dates, and serial number.
components.analogy: The passport itself — an identity document anyone can verify.

components.role: Root CA signs intermediate CAs, which sign end-entity certificates. A verifier chains upward to a trusted root.
components.analogy: A reference vouched for by someone who is in turn vouched for by someone you already trust.

subtopics.real_life_scenario: An IS auditor reviews a company's internal PKI and finds the root CA's private key stored on an always-online, internet-connected server 'for convenience'. This is a critical finding: a single compromise of that key would let an attacker forge a trusted certificate for any system in the company. The recommendation — move the root CA offline (air-gapped and powered down) and issue day-to-day certificates only from intermediate CAs.
common_mistakes: Thinking the CA stores or sees private keys. The subject generates its own key pair and keeps the private key; the CA only signs the public key.
Believing a certificate proves the holder is trustworthy. It only proves the public key belongs to the named identity — the CA vouches for identity, not for honesty.
Treating the root and intermediate CAs as interchangeable. The root is the trust anchor and is kept offline; intermediates do the day-to-day issuing so the root is rarely exposed.
subtopics.exam_tip: PKI binds a public key to a verified identity. CA issues and signs; RA verifies identity first; the certificate is the signed binding. Protecting the offline root CA's private key is the most important control.
subtopics.memory_aid: RA checks, CA signs, the certificate binds. Trust flows down from the root; verification chains up to it.
